title: The open window debate
goal: Explain the open window hypothesis, the case against it, and why athletes' immune studies are so hard to read.

steps.title: The open window idea

claims.text: Innate and acquired immune function are often reported to fall transiently by 15 to 70% in the hours after heavy exertion.

evidence.quote: Both innate and acquired immunity are often reported to decrease transiently in the hours after heavy exertion, typically 15-70%

claims.text: The open window idea is well accepted, though clear and consistent markers of the immune dip are missing.

evidence.quote: The notion that prolonged, intense exercise causes an "open window" of immunodepression during recovery after exercise is well accepted.
However, except for salivary IgA, clear and consistent markers of this immunodepression remain elusive.

steps.title: Salivary IgA: easy to measure, hard to read
steps.text:
[Salivary IgA](g:salivary-iga) is an antibody that guards the lining of mouth and throat. Spit is easy to collect, so it became the favourite [immune marker](g:immune-marker).

It does drop after hard exercise: one study found it low right after 2 h of intensive cycling and back to normal within 24 h [[c:iga-transient]]. But in a field study of the Comrades ultramarathon, IgA in the 4 weeks before and 2 weeks after the race was unrelated to who got a cold [[c:iga-unrelated]].

A marker is a sign, not an illness. A dip in a marker only matters if it predicts getting sick, and for IgA that link is weak.

claims.text: Salivary IgA fell after 2 h of intensive cycling and returned to normal within 24 h.

evidence.quote: salivary IgA concentrations decreased immediately after 2 h of intensive cycling exercise, and remained low in samples collected 1 h post-exercise, but returned to normal levels within 24 h

claims.text: In Comrades Marathon runners, salivary IgA before and after the race was unrelated to the incidence of self-reported URTI.

evidence.quote: found that salivary IgA levels in the 4 weeks prior to the race, and 2 weeks following the race, were unrelated to the incidence of self-reported URTI

steps.title: The case against: Campbell and Turner, 2018
steps.text:
Campbell and Turner (2018) argue that the window is a myth. Their three points [[c:three-points]]:

1. Little reliable evidence shows that vigorous exercise raises the risk of infection.
2. Changes in salivary IgA do not mark a period of suppression.
3. The fall in lymphocytes 1 to 2 h after exercise is a redistribution to tissues, giving more [immune surveillance](g:immune-surveillance), not less.

They add that regular exercise improves immune competence, and that vaccine responses can be higher after a bout. This is a review by authors who take one side, so read it as an argument, not as a verdict.

claims.text: Campbell and Turner argue that evidence for exercise-induced immune suppression is weak: IgA changes do not signal suppression and the lymphocyte fall is a redistribution.

evidence.quote: limited reliable evidence exists to support the claim that vigorous exercise heightens risk of opportunistic infections

reflects a transient and time-dependent redistribution of immune cells to peripheral tissues, resulting in a heightened state of immune surveillance and immune regulation, as opposed to immune suppression

steps.title: Where the debate stands
steps.text:
In 2020 a journal published a debate on the question. Both sides agreed on one key point: infection risk in athletes has many causes [[c:multifactorial]]. Anxiety, sleep disruption, travel, exposure to germs, poor nutrition and extreme weather all hit athletes at the same time as hard training, and each one affects immunity [[c:confounders]].

What is still open is whether exercise itself raises infection risk, apart from those other factors [[c:unresolved]]. Those other factors are [confounders](g:confounder): they travel with the training load and muddy the comparison.

claims.text: Both sides of the 2020 debate agree that infection susceptibility has a multifactorial basis.

evidence.quote: A key point of agreement between the groups is that infection susceptibility has a multifactorial underpinning.

claims.text: Anxiety, sleep disruption, travel, exposure, nutritional deficits and environmental extremes accompany arduous exercise in athletes.

evidence.quote: the many other factors (e.g. anxiety, sleep disruption, travel, exposure, nutritional deficits, environmental extremes, etc.) experienced by these populations

claims.text: Whether exercise itself raises infection risk independently of other factors is unresolved.

evidence.quote: An issue that remains to be resolved is whether exercise per se is a causative factor of increased infection risk in athletes.

debate.question: Does heavy exercise by itself open a window for infection?

sides.position: Yes, in part: heavy exertion lowers immune function for hours, and repeated bouts without recovery may raise the risk of illness.
No: the lymphocyte fall is a redistribution, IgA does not predict illness, and the infections seen in athletes track travel, stress and sleep loss.

steps.title: How to read an immune study
steps.text:
Most open window studies share four limits.

- They measure a marker in blood or saliva, not whether the person got ill.
- Cells are tested in a dish, which may not match what happens in the body.
- Illness is self-reported, and a sore throat has many causes.
- Training load comes bundled with travel, stress and poor sleep.

The link between weaker cell function in a dish and real illness after exercise is not yet proven [[c:link-unproven]].

A fair stance: heavy exercise is one stressor among several, and it adds to the rest. Whichever side proves right, the others are worth fixing, and the next two lessons cover them.

claims.text: Reduced immune cell function in vitro may coincide with illness after exercise, but more work is needed.

evidence.quote: Some evidence suggests that reduced immune cell function in vitro may coincide with changes in vivo and rates of illness after exercise, but more work is required to substantiate this notion.

points: The open window idea: for some hours after heavy exercise, defence is weaker and germs get in more easily.
Salivary IgA drops after hard exercise but did not predict colds in a marathon field study.
Campbell and Turner say the lymphocyte fall is redistribution and surveillance; the other side says heavy loads do lower function.
Both sides agree that infection risk has many causes; whether exercise alone is one is unresolved.
A marker in blood or saliva is not an illness: look for infection outcomes and confounders.

variants.stem: What does the open window hypothesis claim?

options.text: For some hours after heavy exercise, defence is lower and infection is easier
options.why: Right: a short period of weakened immunity during recovery.

options.text: Regular training weakens the immune system for good
options.why: The idea concerns hours after a bout, not a lasting loss.

options.text: Hard exercise makes defence stronger for the next day
options.why: That is the opposite of the claim.

variants.stem: Which observation was a main pillar of the open window hypothesis?

options.text: Resting heart rate falls after weeks of training
options.why: This is a training adaptation, unrelated to immunity.

options.text: Muscle glycogen is lower after a long ride
options.why: True, but not an immune finding.

options.text: Lymphocyte numbers and function in blood fall after prolonged exercise
options.why: Right: this fall in blood counts and in-dish function was read as suppression.

variants.stem: A study finds salivary IgA 30% lower 1 h after a 2 h ride and back to normal the next day. Best reading?

options.text: Proof that a window opened and a cold will follow
options.why: The dip is real, but the link to colds was not shown.

options.text: A short dip; by itself it does not show a higher chance of illness
options.why: Right: IgA changes were not linked to who got ill in the field study.

options.text: Proof that IgA plays no role in defence
options.why: IgA guards the throat lining; the point is that a dip does not predict colds.

options.text: A sign that the rider is already infected
options.why: A dip like this is common after hard exercise in healthy people.

variants.stem: Why is a dip in an immune marker not the same as catching a cold?

options.text: A marker is a sign; illness needs a germ and failing defence
options.why: Right: the dip matters only if it predicts illness, and for IgA that link is weak.

options.text: Markers are measured with errors of 100%
options.why: Measurement error is not the main point; relevance is.

options.text: Illness comes only from the skin barrier, not from markers
options.why: Illness depends on exposure and many defences, which a single marker does not capture.

variants.stem: How do Campbell and Turner read the fall in lymphocytes 1 to 2 h after exercise?

options.text: As a move of cells into tissues
options.why: Right: a redistribution that raises surveillance, not suppression.

options.text: As cells being killed by cortisol
options.why: They argue the cells move, not die.

options.text: As an error in the blood sampling
options.why: They accept the fall is real; they dispute what it means.

options.text: As an early sign of a new infection
options.why: They see it as a normal, healthy response.

variants.stem: On which point did both sides of the 2020 debate agree?

options.text: Infection risk in athletes has many causes
options.why: Right: this was the key point of agreement.

options.text: Exercise alone is the main cause of colds in athletes
options.why: This is the open question, not an agreement.

options.text: Athletes never get more colds than other people
options.why: Both sides took the question of higher infection burden seriously.

options.text: Blood markers settle the question
options.why: The groups disputed how useful such markers are.

variants.stem: Runners report more colds in the week after a marathon than runners who did not race. Which feature of marathon week, besides the running, could explain it?

options.text: Travel, crowds, sleep loss and nerves before the race
options.why: Right: these confounders accompany racing and affect immunity.

options.text: A higher VO₂max among the racers
options.why: Fitness does not predict more colds by itself.

options.text: A lower weekly training volume before the race
options.why: Less training would, if anything, lower the odds of illness; it cannot explain more colds.

options.text: The brand of running shoe
options.why: Shoes have no known link to colds.

variants.stem: A lab study finds NK cell activity 40% lower in blood 2 h after a run and concludes that runners are more likely to catch colds. What is the biggest gap?

options.text: NK cells have no role in defence
options.why: NK cells matter; the gap is in the leap to illness.

options.text: It measured a marker, not whether anyone got ill
options.why: Right: the step from marker to illness was not tested.

options.text: Runners are too fit to catch colds
options.why: Fitness does not remove the gap.

options.text: Two hours is too soon to measure anything
options.why: The timing is fine; the endpoint is the issue.

variants.stem: Given the debate, which stance fits the evidence best?

options.text: Heavy exercise is one stressor among several; fix the others too
options.why: Right: it adds to travel, sleep loss and low energy, and none can be blamed alone.

options.text: The window is proven, so avoid all exercise after a race
options.why: The window is disputed, and moderate exercise is protective.

options.text: Exercise has no effect on illness, so ignore load
options.why: Load is part of the picture in the consensus statements.

options.text: Only elite athletes need to think about this
options.why: The evidence covers heavy training in many groups, not only elites.
